title: TakeMe2Space to Launch India's First Orbital Computing Satellite on SpaceX Rocket
excerpt: Hyderabad startup TakeMe2Space's sub-50 kg MOI-1A satellite, carrying Nvidia Orin NX edge processors, flies on SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission on October 1 with 23 customers signed.
body:
• Hyderabad startup TakeMe2Space will launch MOI-1A — billed as India's first orbital computing satellite — on SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission on October 1.
  • The sub-50 kg satellite carries Nvidia Orin NX edge-computing processors, a 9-band multispectral imager, about 2 TB of onboard storage and a 150-watt power budget.
  • Customers can upload containerized AI models to process imagery in orbit, downloading only the analysis instead of raw data — cutting downlink costs.
  • The company has signed 23 customers across agriculture, mining, supply-chain management and insurance, including US analytics firm Little Place Labs.

Compute, not a data centre, in orbit

Indian space startup TakeMe2Space plans to launch what it describes as the country's first orbital computing satellite aboard a SpaceX rocket on October 1, betting that processing data in orbit will be cheaper than beaming raw imagery back to Earth. The company's MOI-1A spacecraft, a sub-50 kg satellite carrying Nvidia Orin NX edge-computing processors, is scheduled to fly on SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission, founder and CEO Ronak Kumar Samantray told Reuters.

TakeMe2Space said on September 28 that it has signed 23 customers for the mission, including geographic information system companies and educational institutions. Commercial users span agriculture, mining, supply-chain management and insurance; US-based space data analytics firm Little Place Labs is among them.

Context & Background

The business model is straightforward. Customers upload containerized AI models to the satellite, which processes data as it passes over a specified area and transmits only the analysis to Earth. "The customer who sees value in our first-generation satellites is the one paying to download a lot of raw data and then do the compute," Samantray said. "The reduction in the cost of not downloading it offsets the premium they pay for compute in orbit."

Samantray was quick to draw the contrast with the more ambitious "data centre in space" pitches: the spacecraft is an onboard edge-computing satellite running on about 150 watts, while companies like SpaceX and Starcloud plan to use the more powerful Nvidia chips found in terrestrial data centres. Founded in 2024, TakeMe2Space — whose flagship product is called OrbitLab — raised $5 million in a January 2026 seed round led by Chiratae Ventures, with Artha Venture Fund, SeaFund and Unicorn India Ventures participating.

Impact & Analysis

The flight is also a comeback story. A late-2024 technology-demonstration mission validated the core idea — uploading applications, running AI inference in orbit, downloading results — but the subsequent MOI-1 satellite was lost after a launch-vehicle third-stage failure. The team rebuilt the bus and secured the SpaceX ride. The longer-term plan calls for larger networked satellites, around 1,500 watts and 100 TB each, from about 2027, and a 50 kW orbital compute constellation by 2029.

India's private space sector has been racing since the space economy opened to private players, with Pixxel and others winning imaging contracts. TakeMe2Space is staking a different claim — not the data itself, but the compute layer above it — positioning Hyderabad's OrbitLab in a lane with very few competitors worldwide.

Diaspora Angle

Indian-origin engineers power a significant share of the global space and AI talent pool — from NASA mission teams to Silicon Valley chip firms — and Samantray's pitch (a $5.7 million startup taking on orbital compute from Hyderabad) fits a pattern the diaspora knows well: lean Indian engineering teams shipping to global customers. With US firms like Little Place Labs already signed on, the mission also gives diaspora professionals in space-tech a new India-built capability to watch.

What's Next

All eyes are on the October 1 Transporter-18 launch. A clean deployment would validate the rebuild after the MOI-1 loss and move TakeMe2Space toward its Generation-2 satellites. Watch for customer-model uploads and the first commercial inference runs as the next milestones.
